claims.text: Stepwise thermo-mechanical processing that produces SCCPs can simultaneously increase yield strength and tensile ductility in a room-temperature-brittle refractory multi-principal-element alloy family.

A dual coherent precipitation structure consisting of δ-lamellae and γ″ particles overcomes the strength-ductility trade-off by facilitating dislocation transmission and relieving stress concentrations.
The applicable initial alloy contains a supersaturated solid-solution matrix.
The initial refractory alloy typically has either an ordered B2+BCC structure or a dual bcc/fcc structure.
Poor room-temperature ductility arises from continuous brittle phases or from the absence of coherent strengthening mechanisms.
Heavy cold rolling sharply increases dislocation density and forms high-density dislocation walls that support subsequent precipitation.
Annealing at 900 °C produces coherent δ nano-lamellae with an ordered D0a structure and promotes recrystallization.
Controlled heat treatment sequentially forms δ-lamellae followed by γ″ particles.
Maintaining a Ni/Fe ratio between 2 and 4 suppresses formation of the topologically close-packed μ phase at phase boundaries.
Adding 5 at.% Ta, together with adjustment of the Ni/Fe ratio, avoids brittle topologically close-packed phases.
The proposed post-rolling treatment includes annealing at 900 °C for 1 hour.
The SCCP structure contains coherent D0a δ-lamellae and D022 γ″ particles embedded in an fcc-based matrix.
During deformation, dislocations shear through the δ-lamellae and are pinned by γ″ particles.
Slip-band shearing of coherent δ-lamellae accommodates large local shear and relieves stress concentration rather than initiating cracks.
Coherent precipitate interfaces prevent interfacial decohesion while providing substantial precipitation strengthening.
The processed alloy is expected to exceed 2 GPa yield strength and 15% uniform tensile elongation at ambient temperature.
The processed alloy is expected to retain more than 1 GPa yield strength at 800 °C.
The predicted strength-ductility combination is unattainable using conventional thermal treatments or single-principal-element alloy designs.
The strategy should apply to refractory high-entropy alloys in which coherent precipitation is thermodynamically feasible and brittle intermetallic phases can be suppressed compositionally.
The strategy may fail when precipitates are inherently incoherent or the matrix remains intrinsically brittle irrespective of microstructure.
